paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice Paper 37: The Monsoon Drain (Paper 2 §B style)

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
Behind our block ran the big monsoon drain, a wide grey channel of concrete that carried rainwater away from the estate. On dry days it was almost empty, and stray cats picked their way along its sloping floor. Most of the year it held nothing but a thin trickle down its centre, and it was hard to picture it as anything but a harmless concrete ditch. Bolted to the railing was a yellow sign we had all seen a thousand times: DANGER — DEEP, FAST-FLOWING WATER. My mother's rule was simple and absolute: we were never, ever to climb inside.

Paragraph 2
One December afternoon the sky turned the colour of a bruise, and without warning the rain came down in sheets. The drops were so heavy they stung our arms, and the estate's own drains overflowed almost at once. My younger brother Jun and I ducked under the covered walkway at the drain's edge to wait it out. We were in no hurry, and leaned against the railing chatting, certain the storm would blow over as quickly as it had come. Below us, though, water was already streaming off the whole estate and pouring into the channel, so that the empty grey floor began, quietly, to disappear.

Paragraph 3
Jun was bouncing his small red ball against the wall when it slipped from his fingers, hopped over the low kerb, and rolled down the concrete slope, coming to rest on a ledge just above the rising water. 'Leave it!' I shouted, suddenly cold with worry, but he was already scrambling down after it, certain he could snatch it back in a second and not seeing how fast the water below him was climbing.

Paragraph 4
Then the water surged. A wall of churning brown water came sweeping down the channel, rose over the ledge in an instant, and knocked Jun off his feet. The current clawed at his legs, dragging him along the base of the slope; he scrabbled for a hold on the wet concrete and could not find one. His mouth opened but I could not hear his cry above the roar.

Paragraph 5
I threw myself flat on the wet concrete lip and shot my arm down, catching his wrist just as he was pulled past. His skin was slick with rain and my grip kept slipping; the water hauled at him with a strength I could not fight, as though something below were determined to have him. 'Help!' I screamed, and an uncle from the coffee shop came running and seized me by the ankles.

Paragraph 6
Between us we dragged Jun up the slope and over the edge, and the three of us collapsed onto the wet grass. Below, the drain thundered on, brim-full now from wall to wall, the little red ball nowhere to be seen. Jun was shaking and coughing up water, but he was breathing, and he was on the grass beside me, and that was everything. For a long moment none of us could speak. We only lay there, the rain falling on our faces, listening to the sound of our own ragged breathing.

Paragraph 7
I had walked past that yellow sign for as long as I could remember without once truly reading it. That afternoon I understood every word on it. Jun never went near the drain again, and neither did I. Some lessons are not learned slowly, over years; they are burned into you in a single, terrible minute, and they never leave.

(Glossary: monsoon drain: a large open concrete canal that channels away Singapore's heavy tropical rain; usually nearly dry, it can fill dangerously fast during a downpour.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, what did the yellow sign on the railing warn about? [1]
questions.answer: danger — deep, fast-flowing water (in the drain)

questions.stem: Q2. From Paragraph 3, why did Jun climb down into the drain? [1]
questions.answer: to get back his small red ball, which had rolled down onto a ledge

questions.stem: Q3. What does the word 'surged' in 'Then the water surged' (Paragraph 4) suggest about how the water moved? [1]
questions.answer: it rose and rushed forward suddenly and powerfully

questions.stem: Q4. What does the word 'slick' in 'His skin was slick with rain' (Paragraph 5) suggest about Jun's skin? [1]
Q5. What does the phrase 'picked their way' in 'stray cats picked their way along its sloping floor' (Paragraph 1) suggest about how the cats moved? [1]
questions.answer: they moved slowly and carefully / delicately, choosing each step

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain why the narrator threw himself flat on the concrete lip of the drain rather than climbing down after Jun. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (position/leverage) — the answer must refer to STABLE, ANCHORED FOOTING that let him pull: lying flat on the solid edge braced him so he could reach down and take Jun's weight without being dragged in (the uncle then anchoring his ankles extends the same chain). MP2 (danger of entering) — the answer must refer to the FATAL CONSEQUENCE of going in: the water was deep and fast enough to have already swept Jun off his feet, so climbing in would have swept him away too and left no one able to help. A fused answer such as 'he stayed on the edge so he would not be swept away and could still grab Jun' earns ONE mark only; award the second mark only when both strands are separately expressed.

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain why the narrator says he 'understood every word' on the sign only that afternoon. (Paragraph 7) [2]
questions.answer: MP1: before, the warning had been only familiar words he walked past and ignored; MP2: having nearly lost his brother to the fast water, he now grasped from real experience exactly how deadly the danger was. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain why the narrator shouted 'Leave it!' when Jun went after the ball. (Paragraph 3) [2]
questions.answer: MP1: he could see the drain was dangerous — the water was rising fast and climbing up the slope; MP2: a small ball was not worth the risk of climbing down into that fast-filling channel. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q9. What is the effect of writing that the current 'clawed at his legs' and hauled at Jun 'as though something below were determined to have him' (Paragraphs 4-5)? [2]
questions.answer: it personifies the water as a living, hostile creature deliberately trying to seize and drag Jun under, making the danger feel alive and malicious and greatly heightening the reader's sense of terror

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of the contrast in Paragraph 6 between the drain that 'thundered on, brim-full' and Jun 'breathing... on the grass beside me'? [2]
questions.answer: the roaring, overwhelming power of the water is set against the small, quiet fact that Jun is alive and safe, emphasising both how narrow the escape was and how precious that ordinary breathing now feels

sections.instruction: Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's dominant feeling changes sharply as the storm and the rescue unfold. For each moment below, go back to the relevant paragraphs of the narrative and choose ONE word from the bank that best describes his dominant feeling there. Some words in the bank are not used, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: alarmed / amused / annoyed / curious / proud / relaxed / shaken / terrified.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Monsoon Drain' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
